title: Shemot: holy ground (Exodus 3:5)
hookLine: "put off thy shoes from off thy feet", for the place is holy

cards: Lots of homes have a rule at the door: shoes off. Some for cleanliness, some out of respect, some because a grandmother said so. Mosques, temples and many homes around the world ask the same thing.

Out of their shoes, people tend to move slower and quieter, closer to the floor. Moses is in the wilderness with Jethro's sheep, at a mountain called Horeb, on an ordinary working day. He sees a bush on fire.
And when God first speaks to him, right after calling his name, the subject is his shoes.

teach.b: The bush is burning, but it isn't burning up: the text says it was not consumed. And Moses says to himself: I'll turn aside and look at this. That's the hinge.
The next verse says when God saw that he turned aside to see, God called to him. Moses, Moses. He could have walked on; plenty of people walk past strange things.
He stopped. Then comes today's line, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "put off thy shoes from off thy feet, for the place whereon thou standest is holy ground."
In Hebrew, admat kodesh. Holy earth. And it's just desert dirt with a thorny bush on it.
The rabbis asked why God would speak from a scrubby thorn bush, and not a cedar or a mountaintop. One midrash answers: to show that God is with the people in their pain, down in the thorns with them.
The holiness isn't in the fancy place. It's where God shows up, and where someone stops to notice. The shoes stayed with the tradition.
Tradition says the priests in the ancient Temple served barefoot.
To this day, when the kohanim, the priestly families, rise to bless the congregation, they take off their shoes first.
And on Yom Kippur, many Jews set aside leather shoes for the whole day. Shoes are for getting somewhere. Taking them off says: I'm not going anywhere.
I'm here, and this spot, right now, is enough.

how: Before the priestly blessing in synagogue, the kohanim remove their shoes, a rule the Talmud records; on Yom Kippur and Tisha b'Av, many Jews avoid leather shoes all day.

o: the beginning, the first word of the Bible
names, the book that opens with Jacob's sons
Exodus, the Hebrew word for leaving Egypt

games.q: at the bush — tap the pairs.
p: take off their shoes to bless

s: God called Moses only after he turned aside to look
the text says when God saw that he turned aside to see, God called him.
the burning bush was a tall, grand tree
the midrash stresses it was a thorn bush: God with the people in their pain.
the priestly families still remove their shoes before blessing the congregation
the kohanim take off their shoes before the priestly blessing.

games.q: you're a shepherd on an ordinary day. you notice a bush on fire that isn't burning up. what do you do?
o: keep walking; you have sheep to mind.
games.why: Moses said, I will turn aside and see this great sight. only when God saw him turn aside did God call his name.

practice: If you can, kick off your shoes and stand, or sit with your feet flat on the floor, and feel the ground under you: its temperature, its texture. You're not going anywhere for the next two minutes.
Let this ordinary spot, this floor in this room, be the place where you stopped and turned aside.

wordCard.voice: Shemot. The portion where Moses turns aside to see a burning bush and is told: take off your shoes, this ground is holy.

carryVoice: Your line: shoes off, it's holy. The same bush still has more to say. That's two hundred twenty-three.
